clue.text: Type for printing, but not at your request

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a body of type locked in a frame ready for the press
second meaning: a phrase saying the thing is on my behalf rather than yours

explanation.surface: A printer explains that the typesetting was done without anyone asking for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as FOR ME, the second half is a two-word phrase: something done for me is not done at your request.
explanation.definitionFit: In printing, a forme is the assembled page of type clamped in a chase before inking, a trade term.

clue.text: Last flood io ruin an episcopal scat

indicators.note: to ruin something is to wreck its structure, so the letters must be rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: A final deluge threatens to destroy a bishop's throne.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has scanning errors: 'io' stands for 'to' and 'scat' for 'seat', so it reads 'Last flood to ruin an episcopal seat'.
explanation.definitionFit: A faldstool is the folding armless chair a bishop uses when away from his own throne, so a church seat.

clue.text: French historian confounded Queen Anne

indicators.note: confounded means thrown into confusion, so the letters that follow are jumbled up

parts.note: R, for Regina, is the usual abbreviation for a queen
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French scholar is baffled by a British monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Anne looks like one person, but Queen gives only its abbreviation before everything is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Renan was a nineteenth-century French scholar who wrote a celebrated Life of Jesus and histories of early Christianity.

clue.text: The preacher's opening an assembly

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its front portion, so only the start of the book's title is kept

parts.note: the Old Testament book whose title means the Preacher

explanation.surface: A minister begins his sermon to a gathered congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Book of Ecclesiastes is traditionally called the Preacher; its first eight letters are kept and the ending STES is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecclesia was the citizens' gathering of ancient Athens and later the church congregation, from the Greek for those called out.

clue.text: A Pole takes hint on the subject of hors d'oeuvres

parts.note: taken as written
N is the north pole
a tip is a piece of advice
as to means concerning

explanation.surface: A Polish man gets a suggestion about the starters.
explanation.walkthrough: Pole looks like a nationality, but it is a magnetic pole, giving N.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasto is the Italian course of small savoury dishes served before the meal, the same thing as French starters.

clue.text: A derisive cry from an Indian servant

parts.note: taken as written
yah is a jeering exclamation

explanation.surface: A household servant in India lets out a mocking shout.
explanation.definitionFit: An ayah was a nursemaid or maidservant employed by families in colonial India, a word from Portuguese aia.

clue.text: Slave-girl from Stowe opens in "Bottoms Up"

parts.words: Slave-girl from Stowe opens in "Bottoms Up"
parts.note: surface reading: a character from a novel makes her debut in a stage show
setter's reading: the name of the slave girl in Uncle Tom's Cabin forms the first half of the phrase meaning upside down

explanation.surface: A character from Uncle Tom's Cabin stars on the opening night of a revue called Bottoms Up.
explanation.walkthrough: Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin features the slave girl Topsy, whose name begins the expression.
explanation.definitionFit: Something upside down has its bottom at the top, so the phrase describing complete disorder fits bottoms up.

clue.text: Feeble-sounding sort of judge

indicators.note: sounding means the word is judged by how it is pronounced, not how it is written

parts.note: feeble means weak or small

explanation.surface: A magistrate is dismissed as weak-sounding.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is pronounced exactly like puny, which is its origin: it meant later-born, hence junior.
explanation.definitionFit: In English law a puisne judge is a junior judge of the High Court, ranked below the chief justices.

clue.text: One twice dramatically shipwrecked or pierced by arrows?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a name borne by castaway characters in two Shakespeare plays
second meaning: the martyr saint shown shot full of arrows

explanation.surface: A sailor survives two wrecks only to be shot with arrows.
explanation.walkthrough: Dramatically means in plays: there is a shipwrecked Sebastian in Twelfth Night and another in The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare used the name for castaways in two comedies, and the Roman martyr saint is painted bound and riddled with arrows.

clue.text: Looks lovingly at the last of the silk handkerchiefs

indicators.note: taking only the last of something means everything except its opening letter survives

parts.note: fogle is old thieves' slang for a silk handkerchief, used by Dickens

explanation.surface: Someone gazes fondly at the remaining silk hankies.
explanation.walkthrough: Fogle is criminal slang from Oliver Twist; the last of the word is all but its first letter F.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle someone is to stare with obvious desire or admiration, an amorous kind of eyeing.

clue.text: Chew Magna named after this? Of course!

definitions.note: the answer is a racecourse, so this is a hint rather than a synonym

parts.note: magna is Latin for great or large
to champ is to chew noisily

explanation.surface: A local historian claims the Somerset village was obviously named after somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Chew Magna is a village near Bristol; translate both words and swap their order, as 'named after' hints, to get the Paris racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Longchamp is the famous horse-racing course in the Bois de Boulogne, Paris, so it is literally a course.

clue.text: Poet suggests a French dance for the Brains Trust?

parts.note: IQ measures brains; the Brains Trust was a BBC panel quiz
bal is French for a ball

explanation.surface: A poet proposes holding a ball for the panel of a radio quiz show.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brains Trust was a long-running BBC programme of experts answering questions; an IQ ball would be a dance for such brainy people.
explanation.definitionFit: Muhammad Iqbal was the great Urdu and Persian poet-philosopher of British India, honoured as Pakistan's national poet.

clue.text: It's flat and ropy, but could turn into a game

indicators.note: turning into something means changing form, so the letters are rearranged to make a new word

parts.note: a racket sport chosen as the game

explanation.surface: Something feels flat and stringy but might become a sport.
explanation.walkthrough: The game is never named: the solver must guess which game has the right six letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinnet, also spelt sennit, is flat braided cordage made by plaiting strands of rope yarn, used aboard ships.

clue.text: Skin trouble not confined to the bloody aristocracy

definitions.text: Skin trouble not confined to the bloody aristocracy

parts.words: Skin trouble not confined to the bloody aristocracy
parts.note: surface reading: a complaint about a rash affecting more than the upper classes
setter's reading: aristocrats are said to have blue blood, and this condition turns anyone's skin blue

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that a skin complaint is spreading beyond the blasted nobility.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloody looks like a swear word but means having blood: blue-blooded nobles are not the only ones who turn blue.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical condition is a bluish discoloration of skin and lips caused by too little oxygen in the blood.

clue.text: Swift-footed 20

parts.note: surface reading: a fast-moving vehicle, with 20 pointing to the across entry meaning a means of transport
setter's reading: a literal translation of the Latin roots, swift plus foot

explanation.walkthrough: 20 refers to the answer at 20-across, a vehicle; Latin velox means swift and pes, pedis means foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The early bicycle or tricycle, propelled by pedalling, takes its name from Latin words for rapid and feet.

clue.text: Flowery monster with extremely ugly tail

parts.note: an orc is an ogre or sea monster
hideous means very ugly

explanation.surface: A floral-looking beast has a revolting tail.
explanation.walkthrough: The ugly part forms the tail end of the word, following the monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchideous means relating to or resembling orchids, so it describes something floral, as flowery can.

clue.text: Madame d'Arblay's Picture of Youth includes a right intriguing set

indicators.note: to include is to hold inside, so the title wraps around what follows

parts.note: Camilla, or A Picture of Youth is a 1796 novel by Fanny Burney, who became Madame d'Arblay
A taken as written, R the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A novel by an eighteenth-century authoress features a group of schemers.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny Burney married General d'Arblay; her novel Camilla bore the subtitle A Picture of Youth.
explanation.definitionFit: A camarilla is a clique of secret advisers scheming around a ruler, from Spanish for a little chamber.

clue.text: Writer's lost boy

definitions.note: possessive, standing for the writer's tools
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the metal points of pens
second meaning: one of the Lost Boys in Peter Pan

explanation.surface: An author's son has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Lost boy is a capital-free nod to J. M. Barrie's Lost Boys of Neverland, one of whom has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pen points belong to a writer, and Barrie named one of Peter Pan's band of Lost Boys with this word.

clue.text: Mug, beer variety, for one leaping about the Alps

parts.note: a stein is a large beer mug
bock is a strong dark German beer

explanation.surface: A tankard of a particular brew is raised to a mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mug might be a fool or a face, but here it is the drinking vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The steinbock is the Alpine ibex, a wild goat that bounds nimbly over steep rocky slopes.

clue.text: Refuse to enter tunes put up for the councils

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means writing it from the bottom upwards, so the order flips
entering means going inside, so the first word is placed within the second

parts.note: airs are melodies
to deny is to refuse

explanation.surface: Councillors are asked to reject songs that have been proposed.
explanation.walkthrough: Refuse is a verb, not rubbish; it sits inside the tunes and the whole is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Synedria is the plural of synedrion, the Greek word for a council or court, the source of Sanhedrin.

clue.text: Portray a member, say

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the word out and listen, rather than look at its spelling

parts.note: a member is an arm or leg

explanation.surface: An artist is asked to paint a club member, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: Member looks like someone in a society, but it is a body part; both words end in a silent letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To limn is to depict in a painting or drawing, or describe vividly in words, an old artistic verb.

clue.text: It gets you some place

parts.note: surface reading: a vehicle that takes you somewhere
setter's reading: a legal document that transfers a property into your ownership

explanation.walkthrough: Some place reads as somewhere to travel to, but it can also be a piece of real estate you acquire.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a vehicle for transport and the legal transfer of land or buildings from one owner to another.

clue.text: Like Olive, drunk!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an olive with its pit removed

explanation.surface: Someone notes that their friend Olive is plastered.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital O makes Olive look like a woman's name; it is the fruit served pitted.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitted olives are sold with their stones taken out, and the slang for very intoxicated uses the same word.

clue.text: Staff Officer digests real facts, and one for the birds

definitions.note: the answer is the genus name of a bird, so the definition is loose

indicators.note: digesting means taking food inside, so the officer's abbreviation swallows what follows

parts.note: SO is the standard abbreviation for staff officer
the truth is the real facts
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A military officer absorbs the facts and dismisses one as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: For the birds is a slang dismissal, but here it points to a bird classification; the I joins TRUTH inside S...O.
explanation.definitionFit: Struthio is the zoological genus containing the ostrich, the largest living bird, so it names a group of birds.

clue.text: Sound windy in a sewer

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to make the murmuring sigh of wind in trees
second meaning: a dialect word for a drain or boggy channel

explanation.surface: Air whistles and moans through an underground drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like a noun but is a verb here, paired with 'windy' to mean the noise wind makes; the sewer sense is a British dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to make a soft rushing or sighing noise like wind, and a dialect noun means a drainage ditch.

clue.text: Smallest French painter?

parts.note: surface reading: asking which French artist was the shortest
setter's reading: the surname is French for the dwarf

explanation.definitionFit: The Le Nain brothers were seventeenth-century French painters of peasant life, and their surname literally means the dwarf.

clue.text: For whom a poet endlessly wrote

definitions.text: For whom a poet endlessly wrote

parts.words: For whom a poet endlessly wrote
parts.note: surface reading: a muse who inspired a poet's ceaseless verse
setter's reading: the poem's title itself begins with this preposition, followed by her name

explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Allan Poe wrote the poem 'For Annie'; endlessly may also hint that POE is a short name.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe addressed his 1849 poem 'For Annie' to Nancy Richmond, whom he called by this affectionate first name.

clue.text: The Greeks had a word for this sort of poetry

parts.words: The Greeks had a word for this sort of poetry
parts.note: surface reading: the familiar saying that the Greeks had a word for everything
setter's reading: the answer is literally the Greek for word, and names a kind of verse

explanation.definitionFit: Epos means word or song in Greek and in English denotes epic poetry, or a long heroic narrative poem.

clue.text: Topping pull-in for a lord

indicators.note: topping means cutting off the top, as in beheading, so the first letter goes

parts.note: a pull-in is a roadside café, written without the hyphen

explanation.surface: A lord stops at an excellent roadside café.
explanation.walkthrough: Topping looks like an adjective meaning excellent; a pull-in is a British transport café. Lord Ullin is from Thomas Campbell's ballad 'Lord Ullin's Daughter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Ullin is the Scottish nobleman whose daughter drowns eloping in Thomas Campbell's well-known ballad.

clue.text: Unusual perception, maybe near to a worldwide communication system

parts.note: extrasensory perception, an unusual faculty

indicators.note: maybe signals the words are only one possible form, to be rearranged into another

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: Someone with a sixth sense nearly reaches a global network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Near to' looks like a phrase of position but is the fodder; ESP is the standard abbreviation for extrasensory perception.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is the constructed language invented by Zamenhof in 1887 to be a universal tongue for all nations.

clue.text: Governor has a speech on capital cover

parts.note: His Excellency, the title of a colonial governor
an address is a formal speech

explanation.surface: The governor delivers a talk about the city's canopy.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital is used in its old sense of relating to the head (Latin caput), not a city.
explanation.definitionFit: A headdress is an ornamental covering worn on the head, and capital here means of the head.

clue.text: A high spot is vertical

parts.note: taken as written
a peak is the highest point

explanation.surface: A lofty summit rises sheer.
explanation.definitionFit: Apeak is a nautical term for an anchor cable or oar held straight up and down, perpendicular.
